description: Hi, I'm Enes from Türkiye. I build apps with AI and I play guitar, so turning Earth data into sound is a great fit. I'll handle code, AI and audio. Looking for a teammate into graphic or UI design. Beginners welcome; our goal is to build something fun and submit on time. English or Turkish.
summary:
Earthtone turns NASA satellite imagery into music you can explore in any browser. Move a NASA GIBS map anywhere on Earth and a small orchestra plays what it sees. The landscape picks the piece: ocean, coast, desert, rainforest, green lands, ice, city or night. The location picks the local sound, from qanun and ney in Egypt to koto and taiko in Japan.

NASA data layers change the music: warm seas play faster, active fires crackle and heavy rain brings thunder. Time travel plays the same place year by year since 2000, so a change like the shrinking Aral Sea can be heard. Explore by touch lets people who cannot see the map hear Earth by ear.

For the Earth Information Jukebox challenge, Earthtone pairs every visual frame of NASA Earth imagery with a sonification generated in real time, so Earth observations become something you listen to, not only look at. That opens NASA data to blind and low-vision people, to classrooms, and to anyone who connects through music.
details: What it does: Earthtone is a web app that plays the part of Earth you are looking at. It reads NASA satellite imagery and Earth science data, and turns them into an arranged piece of music that changes as you move the map. How it works: 1. The map shows NASA GIBS imagery: Blue Marble, daily MODIS true colour, or VIIRS night lights. 2. The visible view is copied into a canvas and split into 48 vertical columns. Each column gives a brightness, a colour strength and a surface type: water, vegetation, bare land, cloud or ice, dark, or built-up. 3. The whole view chooses one of nine pieces (open ocean, coast, desert, rainforest, green lands, ice and cloud, city, city lights, night). Each piece has its own tempo, rhythm, accompaniment and live soundscape, such as surf and gulls, desert wind, or insects and frogs. 4. The map centre chooses a regional sound: one of 13 regional styles, each with its own scale and instruments, from makam Hicaz in Anatolia and raag Khamaj in India to bossa nova in Brazil. 5. A playhead sweeps the view. Brightness sets the melody, the surface picks the instrument, and colour strength sets the volume. Coastlines bring a strummed chord, and busy landscapes bring in more of the orchestra. 6. Optional NASA data layers are read back from their colour scale and steer the music: temperature, fires, rain and vegetation. Features: World tour, Time travel (2000 to 2024), Explore by touch with arrow-key support for screen readers, shareable links, My location, and Save 30 s clip, which renders a WAV file offline at full quality. A light sound engine keeps playback smooth on phones. Why it matters: Most Earth data is visual. Earthtone gives blind and low-vision people a way to explore it, gives teachers a way to let students hear the difference between biomes and the effect of a drying lake, and gives everyone an emotional way into NASA data. Next steps: Real instrument recordings, more regions, video export, more datasets such as sea ice and air quality, and testing with blind users. Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step; Leaflet for the map; the Web Audio API for all sound (plucked strings, FM bells, a formant choir, convolution reverb); OfflineAudioContext for clips; GitHub Pages for hosting. Code: https://github.com/eenessreal/earthtone Use of AI: We used Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant, as a coding partner. - Code: Claude wrote most of the JavaScript from our instructions: the map capture, the image analysis, the music engine, the data-layer reading and the interface. It also helped draft the README and this project text. - Our part: we chose the challenge and the concept, directed the musical design (what each place should sound like, which instruments and regional styles to use, what sounded wrong and had to change) and tested every version on a phone. - No AI-generated media in the app: there are no AI-generated images, video or audio. All sound is synthesized live by code in the browser, and all imagery and data come from NASA GIBS. - Disclosure: AI assistance is stated in the repository README and in the page's source code. The demo video is a real screen recording of the app; Claude helped cut it, balance the sound and write the captions.
